title: All nine back tightening, with a split on the size of the first move
summary: On 5 November the MPC published an 8–1 vote to raise Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4%. The dissent came from Catherine Mann, who preferred 4.25%. Every member therefore wanted higher rates at this meeting, including all six who had favoured a September hold. The minutes explain why the threshold for action was crossed before new wage agreements showed clear feedback. The initial energy shock had grown and lasted longer, recent activity had surprised on the upside, and several measures of domestically generated inflation had ceased falling. Members who supported the same quarter-point move still differed sharply over the case for another one (minutes, paragraphs 12–23).

Energy contracts averaged $108 per barrel for front-month Brent and 216 pence per therm for UK front-month natural gas over 15 working days to 27 October. These were 38% and 81% above the July Report comparison and even exceeded that report’s adverse fourth-quarter energy assumptions by 5% and 27%. Direct energy effects contributed around one percentage point to September CPI inflation of 3.5%. Staff projected inflation around 4½% in the first quarter of 2027 and around 5% in the second. These numbers depend on a declining futures path and eventual base effects. The 28 October Budget measures were expected to lower inflation by a quarter of a percentage point by the second quarter of 2027, with a small activity effect (paragraphs 3–9).

The two comparison bases are important. The percentage rises of 38 and 81 refer to the July Report’s observed energy prices. The smaller percentages measure the excess over the fourth-quarter assumptions in its adverse scenario. By the time of the meeting, the conflict was in its ninth month and energy supply buffers had been drawn down. Sustained de-escalation could validate a declining futures curve. Recurring fighting, wider disruption or damage to refining capacity could keep realised prices higher for longer. Inflation could eventually fall even if energy itself remained expensive, because the comparison price a year earlier would then also be high. A fall in the annual CPI rate from that base effect has a different implication for household purchasing power from a fall in the household bill (summary and paragraphs 3–6).

Firms faced different clocks. Oil and refined fuel had already become more expensive, but gas or electricity bought at a fixed price could reset later. Other businesses absorbed costs through narrower margins. Limited pass-through into non-energy goods and relatively subdued food inflation could reflect weak demand, temporary protection or both. The committee expected much of the protection to run out if the shock persisted. Firms’ wage and price intentions had moved little since September, yet next year’s negotiated pay could depend on the bills workers actually see when bargaining begins. This is the gap between an observed response and a forward-looking risk that justified acting now for members who still found the wage data reassuring (paragraphs 4–8).

The November projection built in stronger wage and price feedback than the July central projection because of the larger energy shock. The adverse alternative paired more persistent energy prices with an additional source of domestic feedback. The weaker-demand case allowed recent growth to falter, opening slack and limiting firms’ ability to pass costs onwards. One way the latter could arise was through business failures and job losses as energy and financing costs eroded cash flow, a risk Ramsden emphasised. The party bearing the initial loss can therefore change the eventual macroeconomic outcome. If sales volumes hold up, firms may be able to restore margins by raising prices. If households cut spending, the same rise in costs could instead reduce employment and investment (paragraphs 4–7, 10–12, 16 and Ramsden’s statement).

The amount of slack was also less certain. Growth had benefited from exports and activity associated with AI investment. Consumers had spent more resiliently than anticipated, although confidence had weakened. Productivity gains could allow some growth without pressure on capacity. Several domestic inflation indicators had plateaued above levels consistent with target, though short samples and the difficulty of stripping out overlapping cost shocks made that signal noisy. Members agreed that slack had stabilised, while differing over how much remained. The weaker-demand scenario explicitly allowed energy costs and tighter financial conditions to squeeze spending enough to contain domestic feedback (paragraphs 9–17).

Transmission was visible across borrowers. Quoted benchmark two-year mortgage rates had risen nearly 50 basis points since the beginning of September, new mortgage approvals were falling and business lending growth remained strong. The median survey respondent already expected Bank Rate of 4% in November and 4.25% in February, below the forward curve. An actual quarter-point hike matching the survey median says little on its own about the meeting’s market surprise. Markets could still learn about the range of subsequent votes and the committee’s threshold for responding to the next rise in energy (paragraphs 14–18).

That distribution of credit conditions informed disagreement about how much restraint the economy had actually experienced. Some members thought resilient growth and stalled underlying disinflation indicated that earlier policy was less restrictive than believed. Others saw volatile monthly data, continuing slack and an uncertain productivity contribution from technology. A nominal borrowing rate can also imply a different real cost when expected inflation changes. Recent strength in business lending and weaker mortgage approvals thus could coexist in the aggregate. They concern different borrowers and different measures of credit activity. Most members still judged policy restrictive, while questioning whether the existing degree of restraint could return inflation to target sufficiently quickly (paragraphs 10–17).

The quarter-point majority included several distinct views of the next decision. Bailey regarded another rise as arguable unless news eased the risks, then wanted a more conditional approach. Lombardelli similarly saw a case for more near-term tightening if inflation pressure failed to weaken. Pill judged a single quarter point unlikely to suffice and favoured using subsequent wage and pricing data to shape decisions further into the following year. Greene now saw the central outlook itself as warranting the move. She cited broadly flat underlying services inflation since spring, underlying pay growth around 3.5% and credit and output more resilient than anticipated. She distinguished those observations from the still-scarce direct evidence of second-round effects (individual statements, pp. 5–8).

Other supporters of the same rise set a higher bar for extrapolating it. Breeden saw reasons to reserve judgement about any halt in disinflation because overlapping energy shocks and seasonal wage negotiations complicate interpretation. Dhingra wanted evidence that pricing power and purchasing power were recovering and wages and prices reinforcing each other before endorsing a prolonged higher rate. Taylor said the much larger energy shock had undermined one condition supporting his earlier hold. He saw the quarter point as insurance and was concerned that an automatic assumption of repeated increases could dislocate the curve and tighten private financing unnecessarily. Ramsden favoured a meeting-by-meeting assessment of pay, pricing and capacity (individual statements, pp. 6–9).

Mann alone voted for a half-point rise. Her assessment used an estimated threshold beyond which households and firms might respond more strongly to salient prices and a separate approach to credibility. She pointed to September CPI of 3.5%, the projected mid-2027 rate of 4.9%, the possibility that futures overstated the eventual fall in energy and an inflation risk premium in the curve. This interpretation was her own. Greene, for example, characterised the economy as having high inflation but a loose labour market, while Mann’s interpretation of the threshold evidence implied tighter conditions. Neither statistical classification was a committee finding. Their difference bears directly on what wage agreements would imply about scarcity of labour or catch-up for real-income losses (individual statements, pp. 7–9).

The operational entry recorded £362 billion of monetary-policy gilts on 4 November under the arrangements announced in September. November’s vote concerned Bank Rate. A researcher linking yields to the decision needs the pre-release distribution for the rate, votes and subsequent path, as well as the projection issued alongside the minutes. The committee committed to judge the evidence again at each meeting. A higher front-end yield following a fully anticipated rise, if the data showed one, might capture news about that future reaction or the inflation forecast, rather than the current quarter point itself (paragraphs 14, 18–24).

questions.question: Did the meeting surprise investors about the next hike rather than the current one?
questions.detail: Compare pre-release meeting-dated forwards and options with the survey median, preserving each observation’s date. Measure revisions to February and later contracts around the release and accompanying Report. A well-anticipated move to 4% could still change the distribution of later rates if the vote revealed more insurance demand or the projected inflation peak shifted. Intraday data alone cannot separate the simultaneous publications.

questions.question: When did firms start to pass higher energy costs on to customers?
questions.detail: Use the expiry schedule of firms’ fixed energy contracts to separate predictable increases in input costs from changes in margins and pricing power. Track sales volumes alongside product prices before and after renewal. Higher pass-through under strong demand and smaller margin compression would support a different interpretation from loss-making firms raising prices while quantities contract. Separate food, utilities and low-energy services.

questions.question: Does stronger credit growth mean that the effective monetary stance was too loose?
questions.detail: Separate new loans, drawdowns on existing facilities and changes in outstanding balances. Compare firms exposed to AI-related expansion or stronger exports with consumer-facing businesses facing squeezed margins, and compare mortgagors with different reset dates. Strong aggregate credit may reflect investment demand, higher working-capital needs or refinancing pressure. Link those flows to investment, sales and employment before interpreting them as evidence of economy-wide demand.

questions.question: Did a more visible inflation peak reach wage negotiations or only near-term household expectations?
questions.detail: Compare 2027 settlements with each employer’s earlier expectation, the CPI news between survey and negotiation and local recruitment conditions. Account for minimum-wage changes and the composition of employment. A larger settlement surprise for negotiations taking place after salient bills arrive would support the proposed feedback. A temporary rise in year-ahead household expectations alone would leave the strength of that mechanism unresolved.
